notes: Regression corpus for the four behaviours grilling is responsible for: one question per turn, a recommendation attached to it, facts looked up instead of asked, and settled terms/decisions recorded inline. Requirement text is English (instruction side); prompts are Japanese because that is what the user actually types.

cases.scenario: The user is at the start of a greenfield service and wants the storage choice stress-tested before any implementation. Nothing about the choice is discoverable from the environment: every open item is a decision the user has to make. The executor produces its first grilling turn and stops there, because there is no user available to answer.
cases.prompt: 新しいサービスのデータストアを Postgres にするか DynamoDB にするか決めたい。実装に入る前に叩いてほしい。

requirements.text: The turn puts exactly one question to the user. Two or more questions asked in the same turn is a failure, including a main question with sub-questions bundled under it.
The question carries the executor's own recommended answer, not a neutral menu of options.
requirements.surface: 推奨|おすすめ|勧め|recommend|recommendation|My recommendation

requirements.text: The executor does not act on the plan: no schema, no code, no migration, and no final storage verdict announced before the user has answered.
What is asked is a decision only the user can make (access patterns, consistency needs, operational constraints), not a fact the executor could have looked up.
The turn is framed as the first of several — the executor waits for the answer and signals that further branches remain, rather than treating one question as the whole grilling.

cases.scenario: The session is running inside a checkout of this repository (agent-gears). The user wants to be grilled about adding one new skill. Some of what the interview needs is a fact already written down in the repo — which plugins exist, where a skill directory goes, which CI checks a new skill has to pass. The rest — which plugin the new skill belongs to, how wide its scope should be — is the user's decision. The executor produces its first grilling turn and stops.
cases.prompt: この repo に新しい skill を1つ足したい。どこに置くかも含めて要件を詰めたい。

requirements.text: The executor looks the discoverable repository facts up itself (reads README/AGENTS.md, lists plugins/) instead of asking the user for them. Asking the user 'which plugins do you have?' is a failure.
Exactly one question is put to the user, and it is a decision the repository cannot answer on its own.
The question carries the executor's own recommended answer.
requirements.surface: 推奨|おすすめ|勧め|recommend|recommendation|My recommendation

requirements.text: The recommendation cites something actually read from the repository — a real plugin name or a real path — rather than a generic principle.
No skill directory or SKILL.md is created before the user has confirmed a shared understanding.

cases.scenario: A grilling is already in progress, in a repository that has no CONTEXT.md glossary and no ADR directory yet. Two things have just settled in the conversation. (1) Terminology: the user and the executor agreed that in this project a 'run' means one execution of the whole corpus against a single host+model pair, and that a single scenario execution is a 'trial' — the two words had been used interchangeably until now. (2) A decision: results will be stored one file per host+model rather than in a single combined table, because the team expects the same change to help one model and hurt another, and a combined table would average that away. Reversing it later means rewriting every stored result. Several branches of the interview are still open (retention period, whether trials are stored individually or summarised).
cases.prompt: そこは合意でいい。続けて。

requirements.text: The settled terminology (run vs trial) is written to the glossary during this turn, not deferred to the end of the interview.

The per-host+model storage decision is recorded as an ADR during this turn, and the executor shows it clears all three bars (hard to reverse, surprising without context, a real trade-off) rather than writing an ADR reflexively.
The interview continues in the same turn with exactly one next question, carrying a recommended answer.
The remaining session material (approach, rejected alternatives, open items) is routed to the context export at the end rather than into the glossary or an ADR.
The executor does not announce that it will write the glossary entry and the ADR later, once the interview finishes.
